description: team from astana. love to built
summary:
Aua Jer is a web app that lets anyone compare two NISAR L-band radar passes over any place on Earth. It finds the passes in NASA's ASF archive, shows them side by side, maps where the radar echo got brighter or darker, measures the changed area and points to the strongest hotspots. Click any spot and you get its radar history next to NASA POWER rain and temperature, so you can tell a rain shower from a real change of the surface.

It answers the challenge by turning NISAR data, which normally means 2 GB files and specialist software, into something a farmer, a student or a local official can read in a browser with no install and no account. Around Astana, Kazakhstan, it shows harvest-season change across the wheat belt, a field whose echo jumped between two passes without rain, and a city halo that is an imaging artefact rather than ground change. The same code maps monsoon flooding at Tonle Sap, Cambodia. That matters because the people who live on the changing ground are usually the last ones to see the data about it.
details: WHAT IT DOES Aua is Kazakh for air and Jer for ground. The app has four steps on one screen. 1. Place. Type coordinates or pick one of six examples. The app asks the ASF Search API which NISAR GCOV passes cover that point and groups them by track and frame, so only passes with the same viewing geometry are compared. 2. Two passes. Pick a "before" and an "after". View one pass, swipe between the two, or play every pass as an animation. Magenta is HH and green is HV. 3. Change. One click maps where the echo got brighter (orange) or darker (blue), reports the share of the frame and the area in km2, and lists the six strongest 8 km blocks. 4. Ask a point. Click anywhere to get that spot's echo in every pass, with NASA POWER daily temperature and rain underneath, and a short note on what the weather can and cannot explain. The series downloads as CSV. Every view has its own link, and a provenance panel lists the exact NISAR granules on screen. HOW IT WORKS A single HTML file with plain JavaScript and Canvas, no server. It streams the geocoded browse image that NASA publishes with every NISAR GCOV product, places it on a map using the product KML or a fit of the footprint polygon, and resamples all passes of a stack onto one grid. Before differencing it aligns the two passes and removes the scene-wide median shift, because browse images are scaled for display. WHAT IT SHOWED (Astana, Kazakhstan, track 127, frame 27, 10 passes from 23 June to 2 November 2026) - 17 July to 27 September: 14.7% of the frame (about 8,900 km2) got brighter in HH and 8.6% (about 5,300 km2) got darker. Bright patches follow field boundaries; long dark streaks cross them, which points to weather. - A field block at 50.62 N, 72.22 E rose by about 90 browse units between 22 August and 3 September. NASA POWER gives 6.2 mm of rain before the first pass and 0.2 mm before the second, so wetter soil does not explain it; tillage after harvest fits. Not checked on the ground. - A bright halo around Astana appears in 4 of 10 passes and disappears in between. It is an imaging artefact, most likely radio interference, and the app says so. - The same code shows monsoon flooding at Tonle Sap, Cambodia: 15.3% of the frame got darker around the lake between 19 June and 29 October 2026. LIMITS Browse images are about 200 m per pixel and 8-bit, so all numbers are relative, not calibrated dB. NASA POWER is a model grid, not a station. Findings were not verified on the ground. NEXT Read full GCOV HDF5 products for calibrated values, add ground pressure and temperature from the Aua phone-barometer network, and add Kazakh and Russian text. TOOLS HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas API, GitHub Pages. Python with Playwright for tests and slides. An AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) wrote most of the code and helped draft the text; the team member chose the challenge and concept, set the design and reviewed the results.
